claim: Overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is known to mediate glutamate excitotoxicity in neurological diseases.
source: Overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is known to mediate glutamate excitotoxicity in neurological diseases.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ROS and glutamate excitotoxicity in neurological diseases.

claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity triggers a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop to sculpt the motor system.
source: We show that glutamate excitotoxicity triggers a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop to sculpt the motor system.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Excitotoxicity initially elevates ROS, thereby inactivating cholinergic interneurons.
source: Excitotoxicity initially elevates ROS, thereby inactivating cholinergic interneurons and consequently changing CPG output activity to overexcite motor neurons and muscles.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Tonic motor neuron stimulation boosts muscular ROS.
source: Remarkably, tonic motor neuron stimulation boosts muscular ROS, gradually dampening muscle contractility to feedback-enhance ROS accumulation in the CPG circuit and subsequently exacerbate circuit dysfunction.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Excess premotor excitation of motor neurons promotes ROS-activated stress signaling that alters neuromuscular junction architecture.
source: Ultimately, excess premotor excitation of motor neurons promotes ROS-activated stress signaling that alters neuromuscular junction architecture.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: ROS are generated as the by-product of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are generated as the by-product of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (Adam-Vizi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Adam-Vizi, 2005.

claim: In the central nervous system, under physiological conditions, high energy demand results in higher levels of ROS production relative to those in other body parts.
source: In the central nervous system, under physiological conditions, high energy demand results in higher levels of ROS production relative to those in other body parts.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ROS production in the CNS.

claim: Endogenously generated ROS regulate neuronal polarity, growth cone pathfinding, neuronal development, synaptic plasticity, and neural circuit tuning.
source: In the past, endogenously generated ROS were recognized as signaling molecules that regulate a range of nervous system processes, including neuronal polarity, growth cone pathfinding, neuronal development, synaptic plasticity, and neural circuit tuning (Li et al., 2016; Oswald et al., 2018a; Oswald et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016; Oswald et al., 2018a; Oswald et al., 2018b.

claim: ROS overproduction and/or overwhelming the antioxidant machinery can generate oxidative stress in aging and diverse pathological conditions.
source: By contrast, ROS overproduction and/or overwhelming the antioxidant machinery can generate ROS burdens, termed oxidative stress, in aging and diverse pathological conditions (Blesa et al., 2015; Bozzo et al., 2017; Liguori et al., 2018; Pollari et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Zhao and Zhao, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Excess ROS causes the malfunction and overactivation of ROS-regulated cell signaling pathways.
source: In turn, excess ROS causes the malfunction and overactivation of ROS-regulated cell signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the effects of excess ROS.

claim: The highly oxidative properties of ROS are damaging to nucleotides, proteins, and lipids, eventually leading to neuronal dysfunction or demise.
source: Moreover, the highly oxidative properties of ROS are damaging to nucleotides, proteins, and lipids, eventually leading to neuronal dysfunction or demise.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ROS damage.

claim: Glutamate acts as the major excitatory neurotransmitter that regulates nearly all activities of the nervous system.
source: Glutamate acts as the major excitatory neurotransmitter that regulates nearly all activities of the nervous system, with a tight balance between glutamate release and reuptake keeping the micromolar concentration of extracellular glutamate low (Lewerenz and Maher, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lewerenz and Maher, 2015.

claim: Accumulation of extrasynaptic glutamate results in glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity to the nervous system in diseases.
source: In diseases, accumulation of extrasynaptic glutamate results in glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity to the nervous system (Dong et al., 2009; Mehta et al., 2013; Van Den Bosch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2009; Mehta et al., 2013; Van Den Bosch et al., 2006.

claim: Dysfunction of Na+/K+-dependent excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs) is a key element of glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity.
source: Dysfunction of Na+/K+-dependent excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs) is a key element of glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity (Lewerenz and Maher, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lewerenz and Maher, 2015.

claim: In mammals, there are five EAAT subtypes: EAAT1 (GLAST), EAAT2 (GLT1), EAAT3 (EAAC1), EAAT4, and EAAT5.
source: In mammals, there are five EAAT subtypes, that is EAAT1 (GLAST), EAAT2 (GLT1), EAAT3 (EAAC1), EAAT4, and EAAT5 (Vandenberg and Ryan, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vandenberg and Ryan, 2013.

claim: EAAT3, EAAT4 and EAAT5 are expressed in neurons.
source: EAAT3, EAAT4 and EAAT5 are expressed in neurons, whereas EAAT1 and EAAT2 are mainly present in astrocytes, where they are enriched in astrocyte terminal processes that form tripartite synapses with neurons and where they take up approximately 90% of released glutamate.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about EAAT expression patterns.

claim: EAAT1 and EAAT2 are mainly present in astrocytes and take up approximately 90% of released glutamate.
source: EAAT3, EAAT4 and EAAT5 are expressed in neurons, whereas EAAT1 and EAAT2 are mainly present in astrocytes, where they are enriched in astrocyte terminal processes that form tripartite synapses with neurons and where they take up approximately 90% of released glutamate.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about EAAT1 and EAAT2 function.

claim: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity can trigger bulk Ca2+ influx into postsynaptic neurons via NMDA receptors.
source: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity can trigger bulk Ca2+ influx into postsynaptic neurons via NMDA receptors, which causes mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, along with other cellular responses, and which subsequently generates excess amounts of ROS (Peng and Jou, 2010; Prentice et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peng and Jou, 2010; Prentice et al., 2015.

claim: Dysregulation of neural circuit activity can initiate subsequent disruption of the integrity of other constituents in the same network, resulting in overall circuit dysfunction and even neurodegeneration.
source: Notably, it has emerged that dysregulation of neural circuit activity can initiate subsequent disruption of the integrity of other constituents in the same network, resulting in overall circuit dysfunction and even neurodegeneration (Fornito et al., 2015; Hussain et al., 2018; Palop and Mucke, 2010; Shababi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fornito et al., 2015; Hussain et al., 2018; Palop and Mucke, 2010; Shababi et al., 2014.

claim: Coordinated animal behaviors are linked to the activity of spinal cord central pattern generators (CPG).
source: Coordinated animal behaviors are linked to the activity of spinal cord central pattern generators (CPG), which are known to be specialized circuits that integrate inputs from the central brain and sensory neurons, and that subsequently generate rhythmic and patterned outputs to motor neurons (Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kiehn, 2016.

claim: The Drosophila feed-forward locomotor circuit has served as an appropriate model for exploring the pathogenic network mechanisms that underlie neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The Drosophila feed-forward locomotor circuit has served as an appropriate model for exploring the pathogenic network mechanisms that underlie neurodegenerative diseases (Held et al., 2019; Imlach et al., 2012; Lotti et al., 2012), because it has a relatively simple neural circuitry compared to mammals yet retains conserved functions (Clark et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Held et al., 2019; Imlach et al., 2012; Lotti et al., 2012; Clark et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2017.

claim: Drosophila Eaat1 is the sole Drosophila homolog of human EAAT2.
source: Interestingly, we found that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity due to depletion of Drosophila Eaat1, the sole Drosophila homolog of human EAAT2 (Besson et al., 2000), can induce a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop that impairs the proper activities of the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles, ultimately leading to motor neuron overexcitation, abnormal NMJ growth and strength, and compromised movement.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Besson et al., 2000.

claim: Depletion of Drosophila Eaat1 can induce a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop that impairs the proper activities of the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles.
source: Interestingly, we found that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity due to depletion of Drosophila Eaat1, the sole Drosophila homolog of human EAAT2 (Besson et al., 2000), can induce a circuit-dependent ROS feedback loop that impairs the proper activities of the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles, ultimately leading to motor neuron overexcitation, abnormal NMJ growth and strength, and compromised movement.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Alterations in synaptic structure and function have been associated with a wide range of chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Alterations in synaptic structure and function have been associated with a wide range of chronic neurodegenerative diseases (Chand et al., 2018; Dachs et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2004; Kariya et al., 2008; Lepeta et al., 2016; Rocha et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2016; Wishart et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The eaat1hypo mutant allele contained an insertion of a roo transposon in the last intron of the eaat1 locus, which results in a severe reduction of Eaat1 protein levels.
source: The mutant allele contained an insertion of a roo transposon in the last intron of the eaat1 locus, which results in a severe reduction of Eaat1 protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: eaat1 null mutants (eaat1SM2/SM2) died before the first instar larval stage.
source: Although eaat1 null mutants (eaat1SM2/SM2) died before the first instar larval stage, as reported previously (Stacey et al., 2010), approximately 20% of eaat1hypo/hypo animals developed almost normally during the larval stages, but most of them died at early pupal stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and supported by a citation to Stacey et al., 2010.

claim: Approximately 20% of eaat1hypo/hypo animals developed almost normally during the larval stages, but most of them died at early pupal stages.
source: Although eaat1 null mutants (eaat1SM2/SM2) died before the first instar larval stage, as reported previously (Stacey et al., 2010), approximately 20% of eaat1hypo/hypo animals developed almost normally during the larval stages, but most of them died at early pupal stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A majority of eaat1hypo/SM2 mutants died between the first and second instar larval stages.
source: We noted that a majority of eaat1hypo/SM2 mutants died between the first and second instar larval stages, whereas ~1% of the mutants could further develop until the third instar stage, but they exhibited a significant ~10-day developmental delay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The expression levels of Eaat1 are correlated with successful larval development.
source: These data indicate that the expression levels of Eaat1 are correlated with successful larval development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing developmental outcomes with different Eaat1 levels.

claim: eaat1hypo mutants displayed an ~50% increase in bouton number compared to wild-type controls.
source: As shown in Figure 1A–D, eaat1hypo mutants displayed an ~50% increase in bouton number compared to wild-type controls, but their boutons were significantly smaller.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A–D.

claim: eaat1hypo mutant boutons were significantly smaller than wild-type controls.
source: As shown in Figure 1A–D, eaat1hypo mutants displayed an ~50% increase in bouton number compared to wild-type controls, but their boutons were significantly smaller.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1A–D.

claim: Overall presynaptic area, active zone number per NMJ, and muscle surface area in controls and eaat1hypo mutants were indistinguishable.
source: Overall presynaptic area, active zone number per NMJ, and muscle surface area in controls and eaat1hypo mutants were indistinguishable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC).
source: Compared to controls, eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC) (Figure 1E–G), whereas the amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants (Figure 1H; not shown for frequency), suggesting that loss of eaat1 also abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1E–G.

claim: The amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants.
source: Compared to controls, eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC) (Figure 1E–G), whereas the amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants (Figure 1H; not shown for frequency), suggesting that loss of eaat1 also abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Loss of eaat1 abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
source: Compared to controls, eaat1hypo mutants showed an increase in the EJP amplitude and quantal content (QC) (Figure 1E–G), whereas the amplitude and frequency of miniature EJPs were comparable between controls and eaat1 mutants (Figure 1H; not shown for frequency), suggesting that loss of eaat1 also abnormally increases neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing increased EJP amplitude and quantal content.

claim: Drosophila larval feed-forward locomotion is driven by the rhythmic activity of the locomotor CPG located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: Drosophila larval feed-forward locomotion is driven by the rhythmic activity of the locomotor CPG located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Cattaert and Birman, 2001), reminiscent of human and mouse spinal cords.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cattaert and Birman, 2001.

claim: Motor neurons that are derived from dissected first instar larvae of the eaat1 null mutants receive sustained locomotor CPG output.
source: It has been shown that motor neurons that are derived from dissected first instar larvae of the eaat1 null mutants receive sustained locomotor CPG output (Stacey et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stacey et al., 2010.

claim: eaat1hypo motor neurons displayed a marked increase (~5 fold) in burst duration.
source: By contrast, eaat1hypo motor neurons displayed a marked increase (~5 fold) in burst duration (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1I–J.

claim: Burst frequency and intra-burst spike density were decreased in eaat1hypo mutants relative to those in controls.
source: Moreover, burst frequency and intra-burst spike density were decreased in eaat1hypo mutants relative to those in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: Control and eaat1hypo motor neurons were fired for 0.28 ± 0.28 s and 22 ± 5.38 s, respectively, per recording minute.
source: To represent the degree of sustained excitation on motor neurons quantitatively, we calculated the overall firing time of extremely long bursts (e.g. >15 s) for each recording minute and found that control and eaat1hypo motor neurons were fired for 0.28 ± 0.28 s and 22 ± 5.38 s, respectively (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Wild-type control larvae displayed coordinated peristalsis and locomotion activity, whereas eaat1hypo mutants barely exhibited peristalsis and showed sluggish movement.
source: Consistent with these results, wild-type control larvae displayed coordinated peristalsis and locomotion activity, whereas eaat1hypo mutants barely exhibited peristalsis and showed sluggish movement (Figure 1L–M).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1L–M.

claim: Eaat1 is required to maintain proper patterning of the locomotor CPG output.
source: Therefore, these data suggest that Eaat1 is required to maintain proper patterning of the locomotor CPG output, and its loss can alter the CPG output pattern, thereby eliciting excess stimulation of motor neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing altered CPG output patterns in eaat1 mutants.

claim: Drosophila Eaat1 is abundant in astrocyte-like glia of the central nervous system.
source: Drosophila Eaat1 has been shown to be abundant in astrocyte-like glia of the central nervous system (Besson et al., 2000) (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Besson et al., 2000 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Eaat1 is not present in the NMJ-associated glia throughout embryonic and larval development.
source: Although glutamate is the major neurotransmitter utilized by Drosophila motor neurons, Eaat1 is not present in the NMJ-associated glia throughout embryonic and larval development (Rival et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rival et al., 2006.

claim: The terminal processes of astrocyte-like glia were close to rather than part of the glutamatergic tripartite synapses.
source: However, we noted that the terminal processes of astrocyte-like glia were close to rather than part of the glutamatergic tripartite synapses, which is consistent with a previous transmission electron microscopy study (Stork et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and supported by a citation to Stork et al., 2014.

claim: Eaat1 maintains glutamate homeostasis efficiently through its close synaptic association in the Drosophila central nervous system.
source: Thus, Eaat1 maintains glutamate homeostasis efficiently through its close synaptic association in the Drosophila central nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing glutamate accumulation upon Eaat1 depletion.

claim: Glial or astrocytic expression of the eaat1-venus transgene fully rescues the motor system defects in eaat1hypo mutants.
source: This approach rescued the changes in locomotor CPG activity, NMJ boutons, and locomotion (Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B). In addition, a similar rescue effect was obtained with alrm-GAL4, an astrocyte-like glia-specific GAL4 driver (Doherty et al., 2009) (Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: Loss of Eaat1 in astrocyte-like glia leads to the defective motor system phenotypes.
source: Thus, loss of Eaat1 in astrocyte-like glia leads to the defective motor system phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that glial or astrocytic expression of eaat1-venus rescues the motor system defects.

claim: Neuronal expression of eaat1-venus in eaat1 mutants can restore premotor circuit activity and NMJ bouton growth but not locomotion.
source: Interestingly, when we also tested the effect of neuronal expression of eaat1-venus, altered locomotor CPG output activity and NMJ boutons, but not impaired locomotion, were rescued (Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: Appropriate expression of Eaat1 in astrocytes is required to coordinate CPG activity between and/or within individual segments.
source: This evidence suggests that the ectopic expression of Eaat1 in neurons can partially restore function, but appropriate expression of Eaat1 in astrocytes is required to coordinate CPG activity between and/or within individual segments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing partial rescue with neuronal expression but full rescue with astrocytic expression.

claim: Expression of the human EAAT2 (hEAAT2)-egfp transgene using repo-GAL4 rescued eaat1hypo mutant phenotypes.
source: Next, we determined whether the functions of Drosophila Eaat1 are conserved in its human homolog. Expression of the human EAAT2 (hEAAT2)-egfp transgene using repo-GAL4 rescued eaat1hypo mutant phenotypes (Figure 2D–I), except for the reduced CPG burst frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: The functions of EAAT are conserved from fly to human.
source: Therefore, the functions of EAAT are conserved from fly to human.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that human EAAT2 can rescue Drosophila eaat1 mutant phenotypes.

claim: In Drosophila, the locomotor CPG network activates motor neurons via cholinergic and GABAergic interneurons.
source: In Drosophila, the locomotor CPG network activates motor neurons via cholinergic and GABAergic interneurons (Figure 4D, top panel) (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002), and motor neurons do not receive direct excitatory glutamatergic inputs (Kohsaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002 and Kohsaka et al., 2017.

claim: Drosophila motor neurons do not receive direct excitatory glutamatergic inputs.
source: In Drosophila, the locomotor CPG network activates motor neurons via cholinergic and GABAergic interneurons (Figure 4D, top panel) (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002), and motor neurons do not receive direct excitatory glutamatergic inputs (Kohsaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kohsaka et al., 2017.

claim: Drosophila can utilize glutamate as an inhibitory neurotransmitter that activates glutamate-gated chloride channel α (GluClα) to elicit Cl– influx.
source: Moreover, Drosophila can utilize glutamate as an inhibitory neurotransmitter that activates glutamate-gated chloride channel α (GluClα) to elicit Cl– influx (Cully et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cully et al., 1996.

claim: Glutamatergic period-positive median segmental interneurons (PMSIs) are responsible for relaying sensory inputs to motor neurons.
source: Glutamatergic period-positive median segmental interneurons (PMSIs) are responsible for relaying sensory inputs to motor neurons (Clark et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2018 and Kohsaka et al., 2014.

claim: Removal of one copy of gluClα did not modify the motor-system defects associated with eaat1hypo mutants.
source: Nonetheless, removal of one copy of gluClα did not modify the motor-system defects associated with eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), raising the interesting possibility that excess synaptic glutamate caused by loss of eaat1 may trigger excitotoxicity to alter locomotor CPG activity, which secondarily elicits excess stimulation of motor neurons.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of vglut-RNAi using OK371-GAL4 lowered excess perisynaptic glutamate in eaat1hypo mutants.
source: Expression of vglut-RNAi using OK371-GAL4 lowered excess perisynaptic glutamate in eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Expression of vglut-RNAi using OK371-GAL4 largely rescued the altered locomotor CPG activity and impaired locomotion of eaat1hypo mutants.
source: Furthermore, it largely rescued the altered locomotor CPG activity and impaired locomotion of eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 3A–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: The locomotor CPG circuit is assembled within the VNC.
source: It has been shown previously that the locomotor CPG circuit is assembled within the VNC (Cattaert and Birman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cattaert and Birman, 2001.

claim: Expression of UAS-eaat1-venus solely in the VNC of eaat1hypo mutants using teashirt(tsh)-GAL4 significantly reversed the prolonged CPG outputs.
source: Consistently, when we expressed UAS-eaat1-venus solely in the VNC of eaat1hypo mutants using teashirt(tsh)-GAL4, it significantly reversed the prolonged CPG outputs (Figure 3A–C) and movement defects (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3D.

claim: Eaat1 expressed in the VNC may modulate the locomotor CPG output pattern, especially burst duration, to protect motor neurons from excess premotor excitation.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that Eaat1 expressed in the VNC may modulate the locomotor CPG output pattern, especially burst duration, to protect motor neurons from excess premotor excitation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that VNC-specific expression of eaat1-venus reverses prolonged CPG outputs.

claim: Eaat1 expressed in the central brain may be responsible for triggering the motor CPG and perhaps tuning intra-burst spike density.
source: Eaat1 expressed in the central brain may be responsible for triggering the motor CPG and perhaps tuning intra-burst spike density.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that VNC-specific expression does not rescue all CPG defects.

claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity triggers bulk Ca2+ influxes to promote mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, overproducing ROS.
source: It is known that glutamate excitotoxicity triggers bulk Ca2+ influxes to promote mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, overproducing ROS (Zeeshan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zeeshan et al., 2016.

claim: Increased ROS levels were evident in neuropils of eaat1hypo VNCs compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, increased ROS levels were evident in neuropils of eaat1hypo VNCs (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: After abrogating excitotoxicity by reducing gluRIID, the increased ROS were significantly neutralized.
source: After abrogating excitotoxicity by reducing gluRIID, the increased ROS were significantly neutralized (Figure 4A–B), suggesting that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity increases oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity increases oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit.
source: After abrogating excitotoxicity by reducing gluRIID, the increased ROS were significantly neutralized (Figure 4A–B), suggesting that glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity increases oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that reducing gluRIID neutralizes increased ROS.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of hSOD1 using nSyb-GAL4 eliminated the increased ROS in eaat1hypo mutants.
source: Pan-neuronal expression of hSOD1 using nSyb-GAL4 eliminated the increased ROS in eaat1hypo mutants (Figure 4C) and also rescued the defects in locomotor CPG activity and larval movement (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4D–G.

claim: Excess ROS in neurons contributes to premotor circuit dysfunction in eaat1 mutants.
source: These results provide evidence that excess ROS in neurons contributes to premotor circuit dysfunction in eaat1 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that pan-neuronal expression of hSOD1 rescues CPG defects.

claim: Expression of hSOD1 in glutamatergic neurons in eaat1hypo mutants using OK371-GAL4 did not reverse the increased ROS within the VNC or motor-system phenotypes.
source: We first expressed hSOD1 in glutamatergic neurons in eaat1hypo mutants using OK371-GAL4. However, neither the increased ROS within the VNC nor those within the motor-system phenotypes were reversed (Figure 4C–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C–G.

claim: No rescue was observed when hSOD1 was expressed in GABAergic neurons using gad1-GAL4.
source: Furthermore, no rescue was observed when hSOD1 was expressed in GABAergic neurons using gad1-GAL4 (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G.

claim: Expression of hSOD1 in cholinergic neurons using cha-GAL4 led to a significant restoration of the ROS level, locomotor CPG activity, and locomotion.
source: Remarkably, expression of hSOD1 in cholinergic neurons using cha-GAL4 led to a significant restoration of the ROS level, locomotor CPG activity, and locomotion, comparable to the effect of pan-neuronal hSOD1 expression (Figure 4C–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C–G.

claim: Targeted expression of hSOD1 in both bipolar and class I cholinergic sensory neurons using NP2225-GAL4 failed to affect the motor-system defects.
source: However, targeted expression of hSOD1 in both these neuron subtypes using NP2225-GAL4 (Imlach et al., 2012) failed to affect the motor-system defects (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G.

claim: Upon loss of eaat1, the excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase occurs in the cholinergic interneurons of the locomotor CPG network, dyregulating patterned locomotor CPG activity.
source: Hence, upon loss of eaat1, the excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase occurs in the cholinergic interneurons of the locomotor CPG network, dyregulating patterned locomotor CPG activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that hSOD1 expression in cholinergic neurons rescues CPG defects.

claim: The Drosophila larval locomotor CPG circuit is assembled during the late embryonic stage.
source: The Drosophila larval locomotor CPG circuit is assembled during the late embryonic stage (Kohsaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kohsaka et al., 2012.

claim: eaat1 is functionally required during the larval stage but not during embryonic development when the CPG circuit is assembled.
source: Thus, eaat1 is functionally required during the larval stage but not during embryonic development when the CPG circuit is assembled.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal rescue experiments showing that larval-stage expression of eaat1-venus rescues locomotion defects.

claim: No overt changes in VNC architecture were observed in eaat1hypo mutants with regard to the number of neurons and astrocytes, the processes of astrocyte-like glia, and the dendritic field of motor neurons.
source: Consistent with these results, we did not observe overt changes in VNC architecture in eaat1hypo mutants with regard to the number of neurons and astrocytes, the processes of astrocyte-like glia, and the dendritic field of motor neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acute exposure of H2O2 phenocopies the prolonged burst duration of the motor CPG.
source: Remarkably, H2O2 exposure could prolong CPG output duration in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5C and F–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F–G.

claim: When the anti-oxidative ability of cholinergic neurons was enhanced by expressing hSOD1, the circuit effect of H2O2 was greatly diminished.
source: By contrast, when the anti-oxidative ability of cholinergic neurons was enhanced by expressing hSOD1, the circuit effect of H2O2 was greatly diminished (Figure 5C and F–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F–G.

claim: Upon loss of eaat1, a mild level of ROS does not perturb the synaptic connectivity of the locomotor circuit but instead alters its activity by influencing cholinergic transmission.
source: Together, these data suggest that, upon loss of eaat1, a mild level of ROS does not perturb the synaptic connectivity of the locomotor circuit but instead alters its activity by influencing cholinergic transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that ROS affects CPG activity without altering circuit architecture.

claim: Oxidization of voltage-gated potassium channels caused by excess ROS can attenuate their inactivation, resulting in neuronal silencing under disease conditions.
source: Oxidization of voltage-gated potassium channels caused by excess ROS can attenuate their inactivation, resulting in neuronal silencing under disease conditions (Sahoo et al., 2014; Sesti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sahoo et al., 2014 and Sesti et al., 2010.

claim: Administration of 4-AP reversed prolonged CPG outputs induced by 0.006% H2O2 treatment.
source: Nonetheless, 4-AP administration reversed prolonged CPG outputs induced by 0.006% H2O2 treatment (Figure 5C and F–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C and F–G.

claim: Acute 4-AP treatment alleviated the CPG output defect associated with the eaat1 mutation.
source: In addition, acute 4-AP treatment alleviated the CPG output defect associated with the eaat1 mutation (Figure 5D and F–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D and F–G.

claim: Feeding eaat1hypo mutants with food containing 2 mM 4-AP throughout the larval stages abrogated the locomotion defect.
source: Next, we fed eaat1hypo mutants with food containing 2 mM 4-AP throughout the larval stages. This manipulation also abrogated the locomotion defect (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Treatment of eaat1hypo mutants with 15 μg/ml N-acetylcysteine amide (AD4) significantly corrected both premotor circuit dysfunction and compromised locomotion.
source: Last, treatment of eaat1hypo mutants with 15 μg/ml N-acetylcysteine amide (AD4), a potent membrane penetrating antioxidant (Liu et al., 2015), also significantly corrected both premotor circuit dysfunction and compromised locomotion (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D–G.

claim: The excitotoxicity-induced increase in ROS upon loss of eaat1 hampers the excitability of cholinergic interneurons, leading to premotor circuit dysfunction.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that the excitotoxicity-induced increase in ROS upon loss of eaat1 hampers the excitability of cholinergic interneurons, leading to premotor circuit dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that 4-AP and AD4 treatment rescue CPG defects.

claim: The RFP/GFP ratio of mitotimer was significantly higher in eaat1hypo mutant muscles compared to control muscles, indicating an increased level of mitochondrial ROS.
source: Compared to control muscles, the RFP/GFP ratio of mitotimer was significantly higher in eaat1hypo mutant muscles (Figure 6A,B), indicating an increased level of mitochondrial ROS.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Elevated cytosolic ROS levels were detected in eaat1hypo mutant muscles.
source: Consistent with this result from mitotimer, we detected elevated cytosolic ROS levels in eaat1hypo mutant muscles, as detected by CM-H2DCFDA staining (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The ROS increase in muscles was normalized after the increased inputs from motor neurons were abrogated by reducing gluRIID.
source: The ROS increase was normalized after the increased inputs from motor neurons were abrogated by reducing gluRIID (Figure 3 and Figure 6C,D) or by expression of hSOD1 driven by nSyb-GAL4 or cha-GAL4 (Figure 4D–G and Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3, Figure 6C,D, Figure 4D–G, and Figure 6E.

claim: The altered locomotor CPG activity due to loss of eaat1 can overexcite motor neurons and muscles, promoting oxidative stress in muscles.
source: Therefore, the altered locomotor CPG activity due to loss of eaat1 can overexcite motor neurons and muscles, promoting oxidative stress in muscles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that normalizing CPG activity reduces muscular ROS.

claim: Muscular expression of UAS-dsod1-RNAi using C57-GAL4 elevated ROS production in muscles but not in other tissues, such as the VNC.
source: Muscular expression of UAS-dsod1-RNAi using C57-GAL4 elevated ROS production in muscles but not in other tissues, such as the VNC (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Muscles of dsod1 knockdown larvae could not contract properly.
source: The muscle contractility of larvae was measured during spontaneous peristaltic waving using a video-tracking system. Unlike GAL4 controls, muscles of dsod1 knockdown larvae could not contract properly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: dsod1 knockdown larvae showed compromised locomotion.
source: As a result, these larvae also showed compromised locomotion (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: When hSOD1 was expressed in eaat1hypo mutant muscles using C57-GAL4, the ROS increase was abrogated and larval locomotion significantly improved.
source: Furthermore, when we expressed hSOD1 in eaat1hypo mutant muscles using C57-GAL4, the ROS increase was abrogated (Figure 6E) and larval locomotion significantly improved (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6H.

claim: Muscular knockdown of dsod1 alone did not affect normal synaptic transmission or locomotor CPG activity.
source: Note that muscular knockdown of dsod1 alone did not affect normal synaptic transmission (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E) or locomotor CPG activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–I.

claim: The increased oxidative stress triggered by tonic motor neuron stimulation upon loss of eaat1 weakens muscle contraction and larval movement.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that the increased oxidative stress triggered by tonic motor neuron stimulation upon loss of eaat1 weakens muscle contraction and larval movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that muscular ROS affects muscle contractility and locomotion.

claim: The contractile status of muscles is coupled with the activation of proprioceptive sensory neurons, through which muscle contraction triggers sensory input to modulate or terminate locomotor CPG output to motor neurons.
source: Previous studies have shown that the contractile status of muscles is coupled with the activation of proprioceptive sensory neurons, through which muscle contraction triggers sensory input to modulate or terminate locomotor CPG output to motor neurons (Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Kohsaka et al., 2017; Song et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Kohsaka et al., 2017; Song et al., 2007.

claim: Inefficient muscle contraction upon loss of eaat1 may attenuate sensory feedback inhibition to exacerbate premotor circuit dysfunction.
source: Therefore, this scenario raises the attractive possibility that inefficient muscle contraction upon loss of eaat1 may attenuate sensory feedback inhibition to exacerbate premotor circuit dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that muscular expression of hSOD1 improves locomotion.

claim: Muscular expression of hSOD1 not only relieved the ROS increase in the locomotor CPG circuit but also reversed the prolonged circuit output.
source: In support of this possibility, muscular expression of hSOD1 not only relieved the ROS increase in the locomotor CPG circuit (Figure 6I), but also reversed the prolonged circuit output (Figure 6J–L).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6J–L.

claim: Treatment with 2 mM 4-AP reversed aberrant locomotor CPG activity and defective locomotion in eaat1 mutants.
source: We also treated eaat1 mutants with 2 mM 4-AP to re-activate cholinergic interneurons, which reversed aberrant locomotor CPG activity and defective locomotion (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D–E.

claim: The ROS increase in the eaat1 mutant VNC was significantly relieved by means of 2 mM 4-AP treatment.
source: Consistent with the effect of muscular expression of hSOD1, the ROS increase in the eaat1 mutant VNC was significantly relieved by means of 2 mM 4-AP treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under the condition of 2 mM 4-AP treatment, the increase in perisynaptic glutamate in eaat1 mutants was not affected.
source: Interestingly, under this condition, the increase in perisynaptic glutamate in eaat1 mutants was not affected (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6M.

claim: Excitotoxicity can induce oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles and can lead to their dysfunction via a motor circuit-dependent mechanism.
source: Hence, these results indicate that excitotoxicity can induce oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles and can lead to their dysfunction via a motor circuit-dependent mechanism, and that the feedback arising from inefficient muscle contraction sustains oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit independently of glutamate release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that muscular expression of hSOD1 and 4-AP treatment affect CPG circuit ROS levels.

claim: The feedback arising from inefficient muscle contraction sustains oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit independently of glutamate release.
source: Hence, these results indicate that excitotoxicity can induce oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit and muscles and can lead to their dysfunction via a motor circuit-dependent mechanism, and that the feedback arising from inefficient muscle contraction sustains oxidative stress in the locomotor CPG circuit independently of glutamate release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that 4-AP treatment reduces CPG circuit ROS without affecting perisynaptic glutamate levels.

claim: Growth of Drosophila NMJ boutons is linked to the excitation status of motor neurons.
source: Growth of Drosophila NMJ boutons is linked to the excitation status of motor neurons (Budnik et al., 1990; Oswald et al., 2018a; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Budnik et al., 1990; Oswald et al., 2018a; Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: Elevated oxidative stress was previously shown to enhance the formation of NMJ boutons.
source: In addition, elevated oxidative stress was previously shown to enhance the formation of NMJ boutons (Milton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milton et al., 2011.

claim: eaat1hypo mutant motor neurons exhibited an increased RFP/GFP ratio of mitotimer compared to that in control motor neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 7L–M, eaat1hypo mutant motor neurons exhibited an increased RFP/GFP ratio of mitotimer compared to that in control motor neurons.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7L–M.

claim: Motor neuron overexcitation elevates oxidative stress in eaat1hypo mutants.
source: This outcome suggests that motor neuron overexcitation does indeed elevate oxidative stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased mitotimer RFP/GFP ratio in eaat1hypo mutant motor neurons.

claim: When excess excitation of eaat1hypo mutant motor neurons was corrected by feeding larvae with 4-AP or expressing hSOD1 using cha-GAL4 or C57-GAL4, the NMJ bouton phenotype was also partially or fully rescued.
source: Furthermore, when excess excitation of eaat1hypo mutant motor neurons was corrected by feeding larvae with 4-AP (Figure 5) or expressing hSOD1 using cha-GAL4 or C57-GAL4 (Figure 4 and Figure 6), the NMJ bouton phenotype was also partially or fully rescued (Figure 7A–E and K).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7A–E and K.

claim: Expression of hSOD1 in all neurons (using nSyb-GAL4), or specifically in glutamatergic neurons (using OK371-GAL4) or motor neurons (using D42-GAL4), resulted in robust phenotypic rescue of NMJ bouton defects.
source: Similarly, expression of hSOD1 in all neurons (using nSyb-GAL4), or specifically in glutamatergic neurons (using OK371-GAL4) or motor neurons (using D42-GAL4), resulted in robust phenotypic rescue (Figure 7F, H and K).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7F, H and K.

claim: Treatment with 15 μg/ml AD4 rescued NMJ bouton defects in eaat1hypo mutants.
source: Moreover, treatment with 15 μg/ml AD4 had the same effect (Figure 7G and K).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7G and K.

claim: The excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase acts cell-autonomously to alter NMJ bouton formation upon loss of eaat1.
source: Hence, our data indicate that the excitotoxicity-induced ROS increase acts cell-autonomously to alter NMJ bouton formation upon loss of eaat1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that motor neuron-specific expression of hSOD1 rescues NMJ bouton defects.

claim: The conserved c-JUN-N-terminal kinase (JNK) stress signaling pathway is activated by increased oxidative stress to mediate a variety of cellular events, including differentiation, survival, and apoptosis.
source: The conserved c-JUN-N-terminal kinase (JNK) stress signaling pathway is activated by increased oxidative stress to mediate a variety of cellular events, including differentiation, survival, and apoptosis (Kim and Choi, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim and Choi, 2010.

claim: The ROS-JNK axis positively regulates NMJ bouton growth in Drosophila.
source: It has also been shown that the ROS-JNK axis positively regulates NMJ bouton growth in Drosophila (Milton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milton et al., 2011.

claim: Removal of one copy of bsk (encoding the Drosophila homolog of JNK) or kay (encoding the Drosophila homolog of c-FOS) from eaat1hypo mutants resulted in the restoration of normal NMJ bouton morphology.
source: Removal of one copy of bsk (encoding the Drosophila homolog of JNK) or kay (encoding the Drosophila homolog of c-FOS) from eaat1hypo mutants resulted in the restoration of normal NMJ bouton morphology (Figure 7I and K).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7I and K.

claim: Motor-neuron-specific expression of the dominant-negative form of c-Fos (c-FosDN) rescued the bouton phenotype.
source: Consistent with these results, motor-neuron-specific expression of the dominant-negative form of c-Fos (c-FosDN) rescued the bouton phenotype (Figure 7J–K).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7J–K.

claim: Reducing jra that encodes the Drosophila homolog of c-JUN had no effect on NMJ bouton phenotype.
source: By contrast, reducing jra that encodes the Drosophila homolog of c-JUN had no effect (Figure 7K), which is consistent with a previous finding (Milton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7K and supported by a citation to Milton et al., 2011.

claim: Restoration of NMJ bouton morphology could further normalize the release probability of eaat1hypo mutant NMJs.
source: Restoration of NMJ bouton morphology could further normalize the release probability of eaat1hypo mutant NMJs (Figure 7N), but it did not have an impact on CPG circuit dysregulation (Figure 7O) or compromised locomotion (Figure 7P).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7N, Figure 7O, and Figure 7P.

claim: ROS-activated JNK signaling cell-autonomously causes abnormal NMJ bouton formation in eaat1 mutants.
source: Hence, these findings indicate that ROS-activated JNK signaling cell-autonomously causes abnormal NMJ bouton formation in eaat1 mutants, and they support premotor circuit dysfunction as being the primary cause of NMJ bouton abnormalities and compromised locomotion upon loss of eaat1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that reducing JNK signaling components rescues NMJ bouton defects.

claim: Premotor circuit dysfunction is the primary cause of NMJ bouton abnormalities and compromised locomotion upon loss of eaat1.
source: Hence, these findings indicate that ROS-activated JNK signaling cell-autonomously causes abnormal NMJ bouton formation in eaat1 mutants, and they support premotor circuit dysfunction as being the primary cause of NMJ bouton abnormalities and compromised locomotion upon loss of eaat1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that restoring NMJ bouton morphology does not rescue CPG circuit dysregulation or compromised locomotion.

claim: Acute treatment of dissected Drosophila larvae with non-competitive NMDA antagonists reduces the initial output burst duration of the locomotor CPG and eventually abolishes all output activity.
source: Furthermore, acute treatment of dissected Drosophila larvae with non-competitive NMDA antagonists has been shown to reduce the initial output burst duration of the locomotor CPG and eventually abolishes all output activity (Cattaert and Birman, 2001), suggesting that glutamatergic transmission drives locomotor CPG activity and positively controls its output burst duration during larval movement.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cattaert and Birman, 2001.

claim: Glutamatergic transmission drives locomotor CPG activity and positively controls its output burst duration during larval movement.
source: Furthermore, acute treatment of dissected Drosophila larvae with non-competitive NMDA antagonists has been shown to reduce the initial output burst duration of the locomotor CPG and eventually abolishes all output activity (Cattaert and Birman, 2001), suggesting that glutamatergic transmission drives locomotor CPG activity and positively controls its output burst duration during larval movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study showing that NMDA antagonists reduce CPG output burst duration.

claim: VNC-restricted expression of eaat1-venus using tsh-GAL4 could reverse the prolonged CPG output burst but not the reduced CPG output frequency in eaat1 mutants.
source: Consistent with these latter results, we have shown herein that VNC-restricted expression of eaat1-venus using tsh-GAL4 could reverse the prolonged CPG output burst (Figure 3) but not the reduced CPG output frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) in eaat1 mutants, indicating that central brain removal of eaat1 reduced burst frequency, whereas VNC removal markedly extended burst duration.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Central brain removal of eaat1 reduced burst frequency, whereas VNC removal markedly extended burst duration.
source: Consistent with these latter results, we have shown herein that VNC-restricted expression of eaat1-venus using tsh-GAL4 could reverse the prolonged CPG output burst (Figure 3) but not the reduced CPG output frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) in eaat1 mutants, indicating that central brain removal of eaat1 reduced burst frequency, whereas VNC removal markedly extended burst duration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential rescue effects of VNC-restricted eaat1-venus expression.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of eaat1 extends PMSI-evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents in motor neurons.
source: Moreover, RNAi-mediated knockdown of eaat1 extends PMSI-evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents in motor neurons (MacNamee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to MacNamee et al., 2016.

claim: Reducing gluRIID but not gluClα in the eaat1 mutant background shortened prolonged CPG output.
source: However, we found that reducing gluRIID but not gluClα in the eaat1 mutant background shortened prolonged CPG output (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon loss of eaat1, glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity mainly contributes to locomotor CPG circuit dysfunction.
source: Hence, upon loss of eaat1, glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity mainly contributes to locomotor CPG circuit dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that reducing gluRIID rescues CPG defects.

claim: Targeted relief of the increased ROS in cholinergic interneurons by genetic approaches could significantly alleviate altered CPG activity arising from either eaat1 mutation or short-term exposure to H2O2.
source: Targeted relief of the increased ROS in cholinergic interneurons by genetic approaches could significantly alleviate altered CPG activity arising from either eaat1 mutation (Figure 4) or short-term exposure to H2O2 (Figure 5), indicating that a subset of cholinergic interneurons, which presumably constitutes the locomotor CPG circuit, is vulnerable to and influenced by the ROS increase.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: A subset of cholinergic interneurons, which presumably constitutes the locomotor CPG circuit, is vulnerable to and influenced by the ROS increase.
source: Targeted relief of the increased ROS in cholinergic interneurons by genetic approaches could significantly alleviate altered CPG activity arising from either eaat1 mutation (Figure 4) or short-term exposure to H2O2 (Figure 5), indicating that a subset of cholinergic interneurons, which presumably constitutes the locomotor CPG circuit, is vulnerable to and influenced by the ROS increase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that relieving ROS in cholinergic interneurons rescues CPG defects.

claim: The effect of the ROS increase on circuit activity is acute and reversible.
source: Our temporal rescue experiments further suggest that the effect of the ROS increase on circuit activity is acute and reversible (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Temporal hypoexcitability of cholinergic interneurons most probably underlies ROS-induced locomotor CPG dysfunction upon eaat1 loss.
source: Thus, temporal hypoexcitability of cholinergic interneurons most probably underlies ROS-induced locomotor CPG dysfunction upon eaat1 loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that 4-AP treatment rescues CPG defects.

claim: ROS, especially those derived from mitochondrial respiration, act to strengthen the neuronal inhibition mediated by GABAA receptors.
source: ROS, especially those derived from mitochondrial respiration, act to strengthen the neuronal inhibition mediated by GABAA receptors (Accardi et al., 2014; Penna et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Accardi et al., 2014 and Penna et al., 2014.

claim: Excess ROS can modulate SR calcium ATPase (SERCA) and ryanodine receptor (RyR) activity.
source: For instance, excess ROS can modulate SR calcium ATPase (SERCA) and ryanodine receptor (RyR) activity (Gutiérrez-Martín et al., 2004; Xu et al., 1997; Zima and Blatter, 2006), both of which control the Ca2+ homeostasis of sarcoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gutiérrez-Martín et al., 2004; Xu et al., 1997; Zima and Blatter, 2006.

claim: ROS exposure can oxidize some myofilament proteins, such as myosin heavy chain and troponin C and, in turn, can impair their functions.
source: ROS exposure can also oxidize some myofilament proteins, such as myosin heavy chain and troponin C and, in turn, can impair their functions (Coirault et al., 2007; Plant et al., 2000; Yamada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coirault et al., 2007; Plant et al., 2000; Yamada et al., 2006.

claim: Proprioceptive sensory feedback plays a vital role in tuning locomotor circuit activity in the homeostatic adjustment of Drosophila larval crawling.
source: Recent studies in Drosophila have also revealed that proprioceptive sensory feedback plays a vital role in tuning locomotor circuit activity in the homeostatic adjustment of Drosophila larval crawling (Oswald et al., 2018a) and in a Drosophila model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Held et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oswald et al., 2018a and Held et al., 2019.

claim: Upon glutamate excitotoxicity, ROS-induced muscle weakness can cause inefficient sensory feedback input to worsen the ROS burden and can negatively impact the functioning of the central locomotor network.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that, upon glutamate excitotoxicity, ROS-induced muscle weakness can cause inefficient sensory feedback input to worsen the ROS burden and can negatively impact the functioning of the central locomotor network.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Under pathological conditions, impaired muscle activity can serve as a key mediator for initiating the ROS feedback loop between the CPG circuit and muscles, which may contribute to network dysfunction in excitotoxicity-associated diseases.
source: Therefore, under pathological conditions, impaired muscle activity can serve as a key mediator for initiating the ROS feedback loop between the CPG circuit and muscles, which may contribute to network dysfunction in excitotoxicity-associated diseases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that muscular ROS affects CPG circuit function.

claim: The mutation in Drosophila spinster (spin) causes impaired lysosomal activity and a consequent ROS burden, leading to synaptic bouton outgrowth by activating the JNK signaling pathway.
source: The mutation in Drosophila spinster (spin), which encodes a late endosome and lysosome protein (Dermaut et al., 2005; Sweeney and Davis, 2002), causes impaired lysosomal activity and a consequent ROS burden, leading to synaptic bouton outgrowth by activating the JNK signaling pathway (Milton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dermaut et al., 2005; Sweeney and Davis, 2002; Milton et al., 2011.

claim: c-FOS but not c-JUN is important for bouton outgrowth under spin loss.
source: Intriguingly, c-FOS but not c-JUN is important for bouton outgrowth under spin loss (Milton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milton et al., 2011.

claim: Constitutive boosting of mitochondria-derived ROS under loss of dsod2 or after paraquat treatment can promote bouton growth, but in that case it requires both c-FOS and c-JUN activities.
source: Interestingly, Milton et al., 2011) have shown that 'constitutive' boosting of mitochondria-derived ROS under loss of dsod2 or after paraquat treatment can also promote bouton growth, but in that case it requires both c-FOS and c-JUN activities.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milton et al., 2011.

claim: Different resources and temporal generation of ROS may be responsible for engaging different cellular signaling processes.
source: Thus, it may be postulated that different resources and temporal generation of ROS may be responsible for engaging different cellular signaling processes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that different ROS sources engage different signaling pathways.

claim: DJ-1β, a Parkinson's disease-linked protein, has been identified as a redox sensor that mediates the mitochondrial ROS regulating activity-dependent synaptic plasticity at Drosophila NMJ.
source: Recently, DJ-1β, a Parkinson's disease-linked protein, has been identified as a redox sensor that mediates the mitochondrial ROS regulating activity-dependent synaptic plasticity at Drosophila NMJ (Oswald et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oswald et al., 2018a.

claim: Downregulation of EAAT2 has been demonstrated in patients with Alzheimer's disease.
source: Downregulation of EAAT2 has been demonstrated in patients with Alzheimer's disease (Jacob et al., 2007; Li et al., 1997) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Rothstein et al., 1995), as well as in ALS rodent models (Bendotti et al., 2001; Bruijn et al., 1997; Howland et al., 2002; Tong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jacob et al., 2007 and Li et al., 1997.

claim: Downregulation of EAAT2 has been demonstrated in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Downregulation of EAAT2 has been demonstrated in patients with Alzheimer's disease (Jacob et al., 2007; Li et al., 1997) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Rothstein et al., 1995), as well as in ALS rodent models (Bendotti et al., 2001; Bruijn et al., 1997; Howland et al., 2002; Tong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rothstein et al., 1995.

claim: Downregulation of EAAT2 has been demonstrated in ALS rodent models.
source: Downregulation of EAAT2 has been demonstrated in patients with Alzheimer's disease (Jacob et al., 2007; Li et al., 1997) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Rothstein et al., 1995), as well as in ALS rodent models (Bendotti et al., 2001; Bruijn et al., 1997; Howland et al., 2002; Tong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bendotti et al., 2001; Bruijn et al., 1997; Howland et al., 2002; Tong et al., 2013.

claim: ALS is a fatal adult-onset disease that predominantly causes NMJ denervation, motor neuron degeneration, and compromised motor function.
source: ALS is a fatal adult-onset disease that predominantly causes NMJ denervation, motor neuron degeneration, and compromised motor function (Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2016.

claim: Spinal removal of mouse EAAT2 is sufficient to elicit motor neuron death.
source: Spinal removal of mouse EAAT2 is sufficient to elicit motor neuron death (Sugiyama et al., 2017; Sugiyama and Tanaka, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sugiyama et al., 2017 and Sugiyama and Tanaka, 2018.

claim: Transgenic expression of EAAT2 improves the motor performance of an ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1G93A.
source: Transgenic expression of EAAT2 (Guo et al., 2003) or treatment with the small compound LDN/OSU-0212320 (Kong et al., 2014), which mainly increases translation of EAAT2 mRNA, improves the motor performance of an ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1G93A.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2003.

claim: Treatment with the small compound LDN/OSU-0212320, which mainly increases translation of EAAT2 mRNA, improves the motor performance of an ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1G93A.
source: Transgenic expression of EAAT2 (Guo et al., 2003) or treatment with the small compound LDN/OSU-0212320 (Kong et al., 2014), which mainly increases translation of EAAT2 mRNA, improves the motor performance of an ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1G93A.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2014.

claim: A recent clinical study testing ceftriaxone in ALS patients concluded that this drug treatment had no therapeutic effect.
source: However, a recent clinical study testing ceftriaxone, an FDA-approved β-lactam antibiotic that can transcriptionally promote EAAT2 expression (Lee et al., 2008; Rothstein et al., 2005), in ALS patients concluded that this drug treatment had no therapeutic effect (Cudkowicz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cudkowicz et al., 2014.

claim: EAAT2 downregulation largely occurs at the posttranslational and not at the transcriptional level in ALS.
source: It has been argued, however, that EAAT2 downregulation largely occurs at the posttranslational and not at the transcriptional level in ALS (Bristol and Rothstein, 1996; Kong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bristol and Rothstein, 1996 and Kong et al., 2014.

claim: There was no evidence for increased EAAT2 in patients treated with ceftriaxone.
source: There was no evidence for increased EAAT2 in patients treated with ceftriaxone (Cudkowicz et al., 2014), and ceftriaxone treatment only slightly increases protein levels of EAAT2 in hSOD1G93A mice (Kong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cudkowicz et al., 2014.

claim: Ceftriaxone treatment only slightly increases protein levels of EAAT2 in hSOD1G93A mice.
source: There was no evidence for increased EAAT2 in patients treated with ceftriaxone (Cudkowicz et al., 2014), and ceftriaxone treatment only slightly increases protein levels of EAAT2 in hSOD1G93A mice (Kong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2014.

claim: The efficacy of ceftriaxone in hSOD1G93A mice is not consistent among different studies.
source: In addition, the efficacy of ceftriaxone in hSOD1G93A mice is not consistent among different studies (Kong et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2014; Rothstein et al., 2005; Scott et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kong et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2014; Rothstein et al., 2005; Scott et al., 2008.

claim: Oxidative stress is known as a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.
